references.text: In [ref:Matt 26:39|Matthew 26:39], we find Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, where he prays: "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me! Yet not as I will, but as you will." This is the closest parallel to Luke's account.

[ref:Mark 14:36|Mark 14:36] is Mark's parallel account where Jesus says "Abba, Father! All things are possible for you. Take this cup from me! Yet not what I will, but what you will." Mark uses the Aramaic word "Abba" and emphasizes the same theme of submission to the Father's will.

In [ref:Joh 6:38|John 6:38], Jesus says: "For I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane expresses this same principle of complete obedience to the Father's will.

In [ref:Joh 18:11|John 18:11], Jesus says to Peter: "Put your sword back into its place! Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" The motif of the cup from the Gethsemane prayer continues here, showing Jesus' willingness to receive suffering from the Father.

[ref:Fil 2:8|Philippians 2:8] describes how Christ "humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross." Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, where he submits to the Father's will, is a concrete expression of this obedience that Paul speaks of.

In [ref:Hebr 5:7-8|Hebrews 5:7-8], it says that Jesus "in the days of his flesh offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered." This is a direct reflection on Jesus' struggle in prayer in Gethsemane.

In [ref:Matt 26:42|Matthew 26:42], Jesus prays for the second time: "Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done." This parallels Jesus' repeated submission to the Father's will.

In [ref:Sal 40:9|Psalm 40:9], the psalmist says: "To do your will, my God, is my delight; your law is within my heart." This messianic psalm expresses the same attitude of obedience to God's will that Jesus shows in Gethsemane.

In [ref:Jes 51:22|Isaiah 51:22], the Lord speaks of "the cup that makes you stagger" – a picture of God's wrath. The cup motif in Jesus' prayer points back to this Old Testament image of the cup of God's wrath, which Jesus was willing to drink.

In [ref:Matt 6:10|Matthew 6:10], Jesus taught his disciples to pray: "Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." In Gethsemane, Jesus himself puts this prayer into practice by submitting his own will to the Father's will.
